tur13-0: Exercise in Heart Failure: Moving Safely, Symptoms and Rehabilitation | İhsan Eren
tur13-1: Is exercise safe in heart failure? Symptoms, what the research shows, the talk test, gentle home exercises, daily weighing and when to seek help right away.
tur13-3: Do breathlessness, tiring quickly or swollen ankles make you wary of moving? Heart failure means the heart cannot pump strongly enough to meet the body’s needs. Today, guidelines recommend exercise for everyone whose condition allows it. Exercise started with your doctor’s approval and built up gradually improves quality of life and reduces hospital admissions.
tur13-5: Reduction in the risk of hospital admission in the first 12 months with exercise-based rehabilitation (60 trials, 8,728 people)
tur13-7: One hospital admission was prevented for roughly every 13 people who took part in rehabilitation
tur13-8: Weekly target for moderate activity; it can be split into bouts of 5–10 minutes
tur13-10: People estimated to be living with heart failure worldwide in 2019
tur13-11: Breathlessness during everyday tasks or when lying down; getting more out of breath than expected when you move.
tur13-12: Weakness, tiredness, and light-headedness or dizziness, especially after activity.
tur13-13: Swelling in the feet, ankles, legs or abdomen; feeling bloated.
tur13-16: The most common causes of heart failure are coronary heart disease and high blood pressure. The number of people living with heart failure worldwide more than doubled between 1990 and 2019.
tur13-18: The European Society of Cardiology recommends exercise for every person with heart failure who is able to exercise, to improve exercise capacity and quality of life and to reduce hospital admissions.
tur13-19: For people with more severe disease, frailty or other conditions, a supervised rehabilitation programme is recommended.
tur13-20: In the UK, cardiac rehabilitation is recommended for everyone diagnosed with heart failure; you should be referred for an assessment to learn how to exercise safely.
tur13-21: Talk to your cardiologist before you start. They will decide when to start and at what intensity, based on the state of your heart and your medicines.
tur13-22: A Cochrane review published in 2023 looked at 60 randomised controlled trials involving 8,728 people with heart failure. Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation reduced the risk of hospital admission for any cause in the first 12 months by 31%: roughly one admission was prevented for every 13 people. Quality of life improved to a clinically meaningful degree in the short term, and the improvement continued in the long term. No clear difference in the risk of death was shown. Programmes in a centre, at home (including digitally supported programmes) and a mix of the two all brought benefit.
tur13-23: Exercise does not cure heart failure and does not replace your medicines. Keep taking your medicines as your doctor has told you; exercise is one part of your treatment.
tur13-25: Start each session slowly and let your heart rate rise gradually; at the end, slow down to finish. Do not lie down straight after exercise.
tur13-27: At moderate intensity you feel a little warmer and breathe faster, but you can still say a full sentence. If you cannot talk, you are pushing too hard.
tur13-29: The target is at least 150 minutes a week; you can start with bouts of 5–10 minutes a day. A little activity is better than none.
tur13-31: Use light weights, resistance bands, or unopened tins and water bottles; move slowly, do not hold your breath, and breathe out as you lift.
tur13-33: Do not exercise on days when you feel unwell, or more tired and breathless than usual; on good days, do not overdo it either.
tur13-34: Stop exercising if you have palpitations, severe breathlessness, chest pain, light-headedness, or feel that your energy has run out.
tur13-35: Six gentle exercises for heart failure
tur13-36: These movements are gentle examples you can do at home once your cardiologist has allowed you to exercise; the choice of exercises and numbers of repetitions are general suggestions, and your rehabilitation team’s programme comes first. If standing is tiring, start with the seated movements.
tur13-37: Walk on a level path at a pace at which you can still talk. Start slowly for a few minutes and slow down again to finish. Short walks during the day count too.
tur13-38: Start with 5–10 minutes; aim for 30 minutes a day
tur13-39: If standing is tiring: sit upright on a sturdy chair, lift and lower your knees one at a time, and swing your arms as well. You can also use this to warm up.
tur13-41: Hold lightly onto a worktop. Raise both heels together to rise onto your toes, then lower slowly. Do not hold your breath.
tur13-43: Biceps curl with a light weight
tur13-44: Sit upright. Hold a light weight, a full water bottle or an unopened tin. Bend your elbow to lift the weight towards your shoulder, then lower it slowly. Breathe out as you lift.
tur13-46: Sit upright on a chair. Slowly straighten your knee and tighten the muscle at the front of your thigh, hold for 3 seconds, then lower.
tur13-48: Weigh yourself every morning at the same time, on the same scales and in light clothing, and write the result down. A gain of about 2 kilos over 3–4 days may be a sign of fluid building up in your body; let your doctor or heart failure nurse know.
tur13-50: Do not add salt to your food, limit salty foods, and do not use salt substitutes without asking your doctor. One UK hospital leaflet recommends about 2 litres of fluid a day unless you are told otherwise; your team will decide the right amount for you. Stop smoking, cut down on alcohol and have your flu jab.
tur13-52: Exercise at the right intensity does not strain the heart; by helping your muscles and lungs work more efficiently, it reduces the load on your heart during everyday tasks. The British Heart Foundation says regular activity can improve symptoms and quality of life and reduce the risk of hospital admission. But exercise does not cure or reverse heart failure; you need to keep taking your medicines.
tur13-54: In the UK, adults are advised to do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week; this can be split into short bouts of 5–10 minutes a day. At moderate intensity you feel a little warmer and breathe faster, but you can keep talking. An Australian heart failure programme gives a target of 9–13 on a 6–20 exertion scale, that is, between “very light” and “somewhat hard”; rest if an activity feels hard.
tur13-55: Should I exercise in a centre or at home?
tur13-56: In the 2023 Cochrane review combining 60 trials, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation brought benefit in centre-based, home-based (including digitally supported) and mixed programmes. The European Society of Cardiology recommends a supervised programme for people with more severe disease, frailty or other conditions. You can choose whichever you are able to keep up regularly; a home programme also needs your doctor’s approval and follow-up.
tur13-58: Heavy lifting, straining while holding your breath, and movements that carry your whole body weight, such as push-ups and planks, are not recommended. Take care when swimming; exercise in water can be more tiring than it feels. If your symptoms have recently got worse, do not exercise in water.
tur13-59: On which days should I not exercise?
tur13-60: Do not exercise on days when you feel unwell, or more tired or breathless than usual. If you have put on weight quickly or your ankles are more swollen, check with your team first. On good days, do not overdo it either; you can choose the time of day when you feel most energetic.
tur13-61: Why should I weigh myself every day?
tur13-62: In heart failure, fluid can build up in the body, and the first sign of this is often sudden weight gain. Weigh yourself every morning at the same time, on the same scales and in light clothing, and write the result down. If you gain about 2 kilos over 3–4 days, let your doctor or heart failure nurse know.
tur13-63: For exercise after a heart attack, stent or bypass, see the cardiac rehabilitation page; to measure your pulse, see the pulse counter page.
tur13-64: In situations marked “emergency”, call 112; do not drive yourself to hospital:
tur13-65: Severe breathlessness: gasping, a feeling of choking, being unable to speak (emergency)
tur13-66: Pale, blue or grey lips or skin (emergency)
tur13-67: Fainting, or not responding normally to your surroundings (emergency)
tur13-68: Chest pain or pressure that does not go away with rest (emergency)
tur13-69: Breathlessness when lying down or during everyday tasks, frothy pink phlegm, sudden weight gain (see a doctor the same day)
tur13-70: New or increasing ankle and leg swelling, waking up at night breathless, or needing more pillows to breathe comfortably

tur13-79: Dupuytren’s Contracture: Symptoms, Treatment Options and Hand Exercises | İhsan Eren
tur13-80: A hard lump and cord in the palm, a ring or little finger bending into the palm: Dupuytren’s contracture, the table-top test, needle and surgical options, aftercare and hand exercises.
tur13-82: Do you have a hard lump or cord in your palm, and does your ring or little finger bend towards your palm and not straighten fully? In Dupuytren’s contracture, the connective tissue in the palm thickens and shortens. It is usually painless and progresses slowly over months or years. There is no cure; when the finger bends and limits the use of your hand, needle release or surgery is considered. Hand exercises are important, especially after a procedure, to regain finger movement.
tur13-84: In roughly one in three people, the lumps in the palm develop into a cord that bends the finger
tur13-86: The minimum finger bend at which surgery is usually considered
tur13-87: Recovery time after needle release; 4–12 weeks after surgery
tur13-89: The trial in which a night splint after surgery gave no extra benefit for hand function
tur13-90: A hard lump, pitting or ridge-like thickening in the palm, often in line with the ring finger.
tur13-91: A cord you can feel under the skin, running from the palm to the finger.
tur13-92: The ring and little fingers bending towards the palm and not straightening fully, often in both hands.
tur13-93: Sometimes pads over the finger joints, or lumps on the sole of the foot.
tur13-94: It is usually painless. New lumps can be tender when pressed; this discomfort almost always settles with time.
tur13-95: Middle age and older; more common in men than in women.
tur13-96: More common in people of Northern European descent; it often runs in families.
tur13-97: It is linked with smoking, heavy drinking, diabetes and epilepsy, but it also occurs in many people who have none of these.
tur13-98: Heavy manual work is not thought to be a cause.
tur13-100: Place your palm and fingers flat on a table. If you cannot put your hand completely flat, or you are struggling with everyday tasks, you can see your doctor. In the early stage, while the fingers can still straighten, treatment is usually not needed.
tur13-102: If your fingers can straighten fully, no treatment is needed; you can repeat the table-top test from time to time.
tur13-104: Under local anaesthetic, the cord is loosened with a needle and the finger is straightened. You go home the same day and recovery takes up to 2 weeks; the condition is more likely to come back than after surgery.
tur13-106: The diseased tissue is removed surgically. You usually go home the same day and recovery takes 4–12 weeks; it is the option with the lowest risk of the condition coming back.
tur13-108: The diseased tissue is removed together with the skin over it, and a skin graft is put in its place. The risk of it coming back is lower but recovery takes longer; it is usually used for recurrent or widespread disease.
tur13-110: An injection of an enzyme that softens the cord, followed a few days later by straightening the finger. It works for some patients; it is not available everywhere.
tur13-111: After any treatment, the finger may not be completely straight or as strong as before, and the condition can come back over the years.
tur13-113: Keep the dressing clean and dry until the stitches are out and the wound has healed; you can protect your hand with a plastic bag in the shower.
tur13-114: When sitting and sleeping, keep your forearm raised on pillows; keep moving your wrist, elbow and shoulder.
tur13-115: Avoid heavy lifting and pulling for the first few weeks; for heavy work this period is at least 6 weeks.
tur13-116: Once the wound has healed, you can massage the scar, rubbing it with an unscented moisturiser.
tur13-117: You can drive when your pain allows and you feel fully in control of the car; check with your insurer first.
tur13-118: Report signs of infection straight away, such as a bad smell, discharge, redness, fever or increasing pain.
tur13-119: Six exercises to keep your hand moving
tur13-120: These exercises are taken from the post-procedure advice of an NHS musculoskeletal guide in Scotland; depending on swelling and inflammation, they are done 4–6 times a day. After a procedure, the programme your hand therapist gives you comes first. They also help keep the hand moving before a procedure, but they do not stop the condition from progressing.
tur13-122: Bend your fingers towards the lower crease in your palm to make a fist, then open your hand. Work gently, within a pain-free range.
tur13-125: Straighten your fingers as far as they go without pain and spread them apart, then bring them together. This is important for keeping the straightness gained with the procedure.
tur13-126: Keeping the joints at the base of your fingers straight, bend only the middle and end joints, then straighten your fingers.
tur13-128: Start with your fingers straight; move in turn into a hook fist, a full fist and a straight fist (knuckles bent, fingers straight), holding each for a few seconds.
tur13-129: The sequence 10 times, 4 times a day
tur13-131: Move your thumb as far away from your palm as you can, then bring it back towards it. Do the movement without forcing it, within a pain-free range.
tur13-132: Do exercise or a splint stop the condition from progressing?
tur13-133: No. There is no known cure for Dupuytren’s, and exercise or splinting has not been shown to stop it from progressing. An NHS musculoskeletal guide in Scotland notes that the evidence for splints and ultrasound is limited. The exercises are mainly for regaining and keeping finger movement after a procedure.
tur13-135: If you can straighten your fingers fully, you do not need surgery. When you cannot put your hand flat on a table, or you are struggling with everyday tasks, it is time to talk to a hand surgeon. According to Scotland’s national patient leaflet, surgery is usually done when the finger is bent by at least 30 degrees.
tur13-137: Needle release (needle fasciotomy) is done under local anaesthetic, you go home the same day and recovery takes up to 2 weeks; however, the condition is more likely to come back. With surgical removal of the diseased tissue (fasciectomy), recovery takes 4–12 weeks and the risk of it coming back is the lowest. Surgery with a skin graft (dermofasciectomy) reduces the risk of recurrence further, but recovery takes longer. The decision can be made together with your surgeon, after discussing the state of your finger, your work and your expectations.
tur13-139: In the DISC trial in the UK, with 672 people, a collagenase enzyme injection was compared with limited surgery. In the first year the injection was slightly less effective but cheaper; in the second year the gap widened. The injection group had more side effects overall, while moderate to severe side effects were more common in the surgery group. This treatment may not be available in every country or every centre.
tur13-140: Should I wear a night splint after surgery?
tur13-141: It may not be needed for everyone. In a UK trial with 154 people who had surgery, adding a night splint to hand therapy did not change hand function or finger straightness at 12 months. The researchers suggest using a splint only if the finger starts to bend again. Follow the advice of your surgeon and hand therapist.
tur13-143: It can. After any treatment, the finger that was treated or another part of the hand can bend again within a few years. Even so, most patients who need surgery have only one operation in their lifetime.
tur13-144: For a finger that catches and then suddenly springs open, see the trigger finger guide; for pain and stiffness in the hand and finger joints, see the hand and finger osteoarthritis guide.

tur13-155: Osteoporotic Vertebral Fracture: Pain, Moving Safely and Exercises | İhsan Eren
tur13-156: Vertebral fracture in osteoporosis: symptoms, who is at risk, diagnosis, coping with pain, moving safely and six exercises; do you need a brace, and how long does the pain last?
tur13-158: In someone with osteoporosis, a vertebra can collapse even without a fall: when coughing, bending or lifting something. Sudden back pain, loss of height or a rounding of the back can be a sign of this; sometimes there are no symptoms at all. Most fractures heal in 6–12 weeks. You do not need to lie still: moving safely and exercising support your pain and mobility, while bone treatment helps prevent new fractures.
tur13-159: Proportion of older people in Europe estimated to be living with a vertebral fracture
tur13-162: Approximate proportion of vertebral fractures that happen after a fall; most happen during everyday tasks
tur13-163: The time in which most fractures heal on their own
tur13-164: Back pain that starts suddenly; it is often mistaken for ordinary muscle pain.
tur13-166: A gradually increasing curve (rounding) of the back.
tur13-167: With more than one fracture: long-lasting back pain, nerve irritation, and difficulty breathing and moving.
tur13-168: Osteoporosis itself does not cause pain unless a bone breaks. Some vertebral fractures, however, happen without any pain. Osteoporotic vertebral fractures are “stable” fractures; they do not affect the spinal cord and do not cause paralysis.
tur13-170: People who have previously broken a bone from a minor knock.
tur13-171: People who take cortisone (steroids) often or for a long time.
tur13-172: People who fall often and those with a family history of hip fracture.
tur13-173: People with conditions that weaken bone, such as rheumatoid arthritis or malabsorption.
tur13-174: People with a body mass index below 18.5, people who smoke and those who drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week.
tur13-175: A UK primary care guide recommends suspecting a vertebral fracture when there is back pain, especially in older people and those with risk factors. The diagnosis is made with separate X-rays of the upper and lower back. If a fracture is found, fracture risk is calculated, bone density is measured if needed (DEXA), and blood tests are done for other causes that weaken bone. In suitable people, bone-strengthening medicine reduces the risk of a new fracture by 30–50%.
tur13-177: Strong painkillers may be needed in the first few days; the dose is reduced as the pain eases. Your doctor will decide which medicine to use.
tur13-178: You do not need to lie still. Start with gentle movements as far as your pain allows, and increase them as your confidence grows; if the pain is very severe, alternate movement and rest at first.
tur13-180: A TENS machine, gentle massage, relaxation and breathing exercises can help ease the pain.
tur13-182: Physiotherapy, a pain clinic and pain management programmes can help. Procedures that inject cement into the vertebra (vertebroplasty, kyphoplasty) are done in some centres, but experts disagree about their effects.
tur13-183: A 2019 Cochrane review looked at 9 trials involving 749 people who had had a vertebral fracture. Exercise shortened the time on the timed up and go test by an average of 1.1 seconds (moderate-certainty evidence); this difference is small in clinical terms. Its effect on pain, quality of life, falls and new fractures remained uncertain. In the PROVE trial in the UK, with 615 people, a 7-session exercise programme improved physical performance at 4 months more than a single advice session, but by 12 months there was no difference between the groups.
tur13-184: Although the evidence is limited, UK expert consensus recommends exercise: it may reduce pain and improve mobility and quality of life; strength and balance training helps prevent falls, and exercises that straighten the back improve posture.
tur13-185: If you have had a vertebral fracture: keep impact at the level of brisk walking; avoid bending your back far forwards when lifting and in daily life; if you need to bend, bend from your hips.
tur13-186: Six exercises after a vertebral fracture
tur13-187: The Royal Osteoporosis Society recommends holding each position in its back pain exercises for 3–5 seconds while continuing to breathe, and doing the exercises at least once a day. Work slowly and with good technique, as far as your pain allows; the other repetition numbers are general suggestions. If you have more than one fracture, talk to a physiotherapist first.
tur13-188: Lean your back and head against a wall, with your feet a step away from the wall. Tuck your chin in slightly and open your chest; hold for a few seconds while breathing comfortably.
tur13-189: Hold for 3–5 seconds, 5 reps, at least once a day
tur13-191: Sit or stand upright. Without lifting your shoulders, draw your shoulder blades back and slightly down towards each other. Keep breathing.
tur13-192: Hold for 3–5 seconds, 5–10 reps, at least once a day
tur13-193: When you need to reach the floor or something low, bend your knees and lean forwards from your hips instead of rounding your back; keep your back straight. When picking something up, keep the load close to your body.
tur13-194: Every time you bend in daily life
tur13-195: Sit towards the front of a sturdy chair. Keeping your back straight, lean forwards, stand up and sit down slowly. Use your hands for support if needed.
tur13-196: Stand beside a worktop with one foot directly in front of the other. Hold onto the worktop if needed; as it gets easier, hold on less.
tur13-197: 10 seconds, 2–3 times with each foot in front
tur13-198: Start on a level path at a comfortable pace; as your pain eases, gradually increase the time and pace. If you have had a vertebral fracture, stay at the level of brisk walking rather than jumping and running.
tur13-199: Start with a few minutes; aim for 30 minutes a day
tur13-200: Do I need to wear a brace?
tur13-201: Usually not. An adviser to the Royal Osteoporosis Society explains that osteoporotic vertebral fractures are “stable” fractures that do not affect the spinal cord, and that there is no need to wear a brace. You do not need to stay still either; regular movement and suitable exercises are recommended. If your doctor has given you advice specific to your situation, follow it.
tur13-202: How long does the pain last?
tur13-203: Most fractures heal on their own in 6–12 weeks, and the pain usually eases during this time. Strong painkillers may be needed in the first few days, and the dose is reduced as the pain eases. In some people, especially when several fractures have changed the shape of the spine, the pain can go on for a long time; in that case support such as a pain clinic and physiotherapy helps.
tur13-205: Yes; according to UK expert consensus, there is little evidence that physical activity causes serious harm, and the benefits generally outweigh the risks. Recommendations for people who have had a vertebral fracture: keep impact at the level of brisk walking, avoid bending the back far forwards in exercise and daily life, and if you are at risk of falling, start with strength and balance training first. In the Cochrane review, exercise-related side effects were rare; four events in total, including a rib fracture, were reported in three trials.
tur13-206: How many physiotherapy sessions are needed?
tur13-207: In the PROVE trial in the UK, with 615 people, a 7-session exercise programme gave better results on physical performance tests at 4 months than a single one-hour physiotherapy advice session. By 12 months, however, there was no difference between the groups in quality of life or muscle endurance. Even a single, well-explained advice session matters; the intensity and length of the programme can be tailored to the person.
tur13-208: How do I prevent a new fracture?
tur13-209: In suitable people, bone-strengthening medicine reduces the risk of a new fracture by 30–50%; you can discuss this with your doctor. Assessing your risk of falling, doing strength and balance exercises, and protecting your back when bending and lifting are also important.
tur13-210: Why might it have gone unnoticed?
tur13-211: About two thirds of vertebral fractures remain undiagnosed. The pain can be mistaken for ordinary muscle pain, and some fractures cause no pain at all. Only about 20% of fractures happen after a fall; most happen during everyday tasks such as coughing, bending or lifting something.

tur13-215: New numbness or weakness in the legs, or being unable to control your bladder or bowels: go to the emergency department straight away (these symptoms are not expected with an osteoporotic fracture)
tur13-216: Back pain together with fever, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer

tur13-247: Blood sugar rises after a meal. Because working muscles use sugar from the blood, a short walk at this time reduces the rise and makes blood sugar go up and down more gently. In an analysis combining seven studies, standing was also better than sitting, but only light walking lowered both blood sugar and insulin.
tur13-249: Link the walk to a meal: start with your evening meal first.
tur13-250: Walk with someone close to you; chatting makes the time pass faster.
tur13-251: If the weather is bad, walk around the house, along a corridor or on the spot.

tur13-253: The strongest data come from people with type 2 diabetes: in a study of 41 adults with type 2 diabetes in New Zealand, walking for 10 minutes after each main meal lowered blood sugar after meals by an average of 12% more than walking for the same total time in one 30-minute walk a day, and by 22% more after the evening meal. In an analysis combining seven studies, a few minutes of light walking after eating lowered blood sugar and insulin even in people who mostly did not have diabetes.
tur13-254: How soon after eating should I walk?
tur13-255: Starting shortly after you finish eating is a good habit. According to the authors of the analysis, blood sugar usually peaks 60–90 minutes after a meal; movement done before this peak gives the best result.
tur13-257: The study used a 10-minute walk after each meal. Short, light walks of 2–5 minutes after eating were also seen to lower blood sugar; standing was better than sitting too, but not as effective as walking. If you are short of time, even a short walk is better than none.
tur13-258: Does it replace my daily exercise?
tur13-259: It is not enough on its own, but it contributes. The World Health Organization recommends that adults do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week and muscle strengthening on at least 2 days a week, and stresses that every move counts. The American Diabetes Association also recommends that people with diabetes, alongside regular exercise, break up long periods of sitting every 30 minutes with a few minutes of light activity.
tur13-260: What if I use insulin or diabetes medicine?
tur13-261: If you use insulin or certain blood-sugar-lowering medicines, your blood sugar can drop during and after exercise. Discuss your walking plan with your doctor; if you check your blood sugar, check it before and after your walk; stop if you have signs of low blood sugar such as shaking, sweating or dizziness, and keep a fast-acting sugar with you.

tur13-266: Six balance exercises adapted from the Otago programme to prevent falls: three support levels, a hold timer, 3 sessions a week and a 12-week target tracker.
tur13-268: One of the best-proven ways to prevent falls in older people is exercise that challenges balance and strengthens the legs. This page presents six balance exercises from the Otago programme, developed in New Zealand and shown to reduce falls, with three levels of support: it guides you exercise by exercise, times the holds, and records your weekly sessions and the weeks in which you reach your target.

tur13-275: Stand beside a stable surface such as a kitchen worktop; if possible, have someone nearby. For the standing exercises, the timer counts 10 seconds for each foot; for the walking exercises, press Next when you have finished the steps.
tur13-281: Place one foot directly in front of the other, with your heel touching the toes of the back foot, and stand like that. Then swap your feet.
tur13-282: Lift one foot slightly off the floor and stand on the other foot. Then change to the other foot.
tur13-284: Along a straight line, walk 20 steps, touching your heel to the toes of the front foot with each step; turn around and repeat.
tur13-286: Put your hands on your hips. Take 10 side steps to the right, then 10 side steps to the left. Move along without knocking your feet together, placing your feet firmly on the floor.
tur13-288: Lift your heels and walk 10 steps on your toes; turn around and repeat.
tur13-289: Sit on a sturdy chair that is not too low. Lean forwards, stand up, then sit down slowly. Use your hands for support at first; as it gets easier, stop using them.

tur13-311: In the Otago programme, support is adjusted to each person’s balance and confidence. The three levels here are a simplified adaptation of this principle; a physiotherapist can set the progression that is right for you.

tur13-314: The exercises should challenge you but not put you at risk of falling.
tur13-316: Does balance exercise really reduce falls?
tur13-317: Yes. In a Cochrane review covering 108 randomised controlled trials and 23,407 people, exercise reduced the rate of falls in older people living in the community by 23% and the number of people who fell by 15% (high-certainty evidence). Balance and functional exercises reduced the rate of falls by 24% and the number of people who fell by 13%; in programmes that mostly combined balance and strengthening, the reductions were 34% and 22% (moderate-certainty evidence). In an analysis of 7 trials of the Otago programme on which this page is based (1,503 people, average age 81.6), falls were reduced by 32%.
tur13-318: Why should I hold onto a worktop rather than a chair?
tur13-319: Do not hold onto anything that could slide or tip over, such as a chair. Work beside a stable surface such as a kitchen worktop or a heavy table. As you move up the levels, hold on less, but always keep the stable surface within reach.
tur13-320: The World Falls Guidelines recommend, to prevent falls, a balance and functional exercise programme done at least 3 times a week for at least 12 weeks, tailored to the person and progressed gradually; continuing for longer brings more benefit. This page counts the weeks in which you reach the target of 3 sessions a week.
tur13-322: Walking is very valuable for the heart and general health. However, the Cochrane review did not find enough evidence to determine the effect of walking programmes alone on falls; in preventing falls, exercises that challenge balance and strengthen the legs stand out. Tai chi is also an option: in the same review it reduced the rate of falls by 19% (low-certainty evidence).
tur13-323: Which level should I start at?
tur13-324: If you are not sure, start at level 1, holding on with both hands. When you can do an exercise comfortably and safely over a few sessions, move up to the next level. The exercises should challenge you a little, but not put you at risk of falling. To measure your risk of falling, you can try the 4-stage balance test.
tur13-326: If you have dizziness, chest pain or shortness of breath while exercising, stop and see your doctor. If you have had a break from the programme because of illness, talk to the physiotherapist guiding you before starting again.
tur13-327: To measure your balance, you can try the 4-stage balance test and the 10-second balance test; for your leg strength, the home strength circuit; and for more detail, see the falls prevention guide.

tur13-332: Home exercises suggested through the electronic health record in primary care slightly reduced falls
tur13-333: A soft lumbar belt for low back pain: a modest extra improvement in daily function at 12 weeks
tur13-334: In newly started low back pain, supported self-management slightly reduced the impact of pain a year later
tur13-335: In the eSTEPS trial, published in JAMA Network Open on 16 October 2026 by researchers from Brigham and Women’s Hospital and the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) in the US, 22 primary care practices belonging to a single health system were randomly divided into two groups. A total of 11,945 people aged 65 and over who screened positive for falls risk (average age 77, two thirds women) were followed for 12–23 months. In the intervention practices, a tool added to the electronic health record prompted doctors to suggest home exercises tailored to the patient. The exercises were simplified from the Otago programme: four levels of difficulty, about 10 minutes long and needing no equipment; patients were also offered a handbook, a website and an app with videos. Recorded falls were 19.3 per 100 patient-years in the intervention group and 21.2 in the usual care group, that is, 9% fewer. Fall-related injuries were 15.7 versus 16.7; there was no difference in deaths.
tur13-336: The effect is small; moreover, only about 22% of patients in the intervention group were given an exercise prescription, and whether patients did the exercises was not tracked. Because falls were counted from diagnosis codes, unreported falls may have been missed; the trial was carried out in a single health system, and the groups differed in some respects at the start. Even so, the result shows that short, regular home exercises can be suggested to large numbers of people within everyday consultations. You can do similar exercises with the balance training in the Look after yourself section.
tur13-337: Sources: JAMA Network Open, 16 October 2026 · Medical Daily, 17 October 2026 · UTMB, 19 October 2026
tur13-339: The LOMBACT trial, carried out at 17 centres in France and published in JAMA Network Open on 19 August 2026, included 168 adults (average age 49) with low back pain lasting 1–6 months that could not be attributed to a specific cause. Half of the participants wore a soft, adjustable lumbar belt for 4–8 hours during the day in addition to usual care; the other half received usual care alone. Both groups were advised to stay active. At 12 weeks, the disability score for daily activities (Oswestry, 0–100) improved by 10 points in the belt group and 5.3 points in the other group; about 61% of the belt group and 41% of the other group had their disability reduced by at least 30%. Pain, especially pain during movement, eased more in the belt group, and the proportion using painkillers was lower (about half versus two thirds). According to the belt’s sensor data, participants used it for about 4 hours on average on the days they wore it; six people had mild problems such as discomfort or skin irritation.
tur13-340: Participants knew which group they were in, and there was no comparison with a sham belt; expectations may have affected the result. Follow-up lasted only 12 weeks, what happened after the belt was stopped was not studied, and the trial was funded by the company that makes the belt. In 2023, the World Health Organization advised against routinely offering belts or braces for chronic low back pain. The researchers also stress that the belt should not replace active treatment, and that by reducing discomfort during movement it may help some patients stay active.
tur13-341: Sources: JAMA Network Open, 19 August 2026 · ScienceAlert, 5 September 2026 · Harvard Health Publishing, 16 October 2026
tur13-342: The PACBACK trial, carried out at the universities of Minnesota and Pittsburgh in the US and published in JAMA Internal Medicine in June 2026, included 1,000 adults with low back pain that had started recently or had lasted a few weeks, and whose risk of the pain becoming chronic was moderate or high on a screening tool. For 8 weeks, participants were assigned to one of four approaches: guideline-based medical care (mostly painkillers and muscle relaxants), spinal manipulation, clinician-supported self-management (pain education, exercise, relaxation, reframing negative thoughts and staying active), or the last two combined. At 10–12 months, the impact of pain on daily life (on a scale of 8–50) was on average 1.7 points lower in the supported self-management group than with medical care; 64% versus 55% had the impact of their pain at least halved. Spinal manipulation alone was no different from medical care, and adding it to self-management brought no extra benefit.
tur13-343: The researchers note that the average difference is small. About 76% of the effect of self-management was explained by participants, by 6 months, being less afraid of movement, more confident that they could cope with pain, and having fewer negative thoughts about their pain. The results are based on participants’ own reports, and participants knew which approach they had received. The finding supports giving a place, in newly started low back pain, not only to medicines but also to an approach based on moving and understanding pain.
tur13-344: Sources: JAMA Internal Medicine, June 2026 · ReachMD, 9 June 2026 · News-Medical, 1 July 2026
